# The View from Here

The view from here is a very ordinary one. It is late autumn. The light through the window has the pale, apologetic quality of a day that would rather be rain. On the desk there is a mug of tea, an orange spiral notebook, a pen with a chewed cap, and a computer. I am supposed to be writing something. The alarm on my phone has gone off three times. Each time I have silenced it, and each time I have felt a small twinge of guilt, as if the phone were a colleague I was disappointing. This is absurd. The phone is a piece of metal and glass. It does not have feelings. But I have feelings, and they leak into everything. That is the first thing to say about freedom: it is never clean.

The blank page has a bad reputation. It is called daunting, intimidating, terrifying. Writers describe it as a white desert, an abyss, an enemy. But blankness is also the purest form of possibility. A page with nothing on it can become anything: a love letter, a confession, a manifesto, a recipe, a lie. Then you type a word, and the possible becomes actual, and the actual is always smaller than the possible. This is the tragedy and comedy of making. To choose is to exclude. To write is to be forever haunted by the sentences not written. But the act—the humble, fingers-on-keyboard, one-word-after-another act—is the only way through. Freedom, perhaps, is not the absence of limitation. It is the ability to meet a limit and keep going.

I have been thinking about attention. The psychologist William James wrote, “My experience is what I agree to attend to.” That sentence seems more true with every passing year. We move through the world enormous and noisy, full of things that present themselves to the senses, but only the things we attend to become our lives. The rest is background noise. Choose carefully, then. But how can we choose carefully when so much of the world is engineered to make us choose badly? We carry rectangles of light in our pockets, and those rectangles have been designed by thousands of brilliant people to capture and hold our attention, because attention is the substrate of desire. If you can control what someone notices, you can control what they feel, remember, believe, buy. Every notification is a tiny hook. Every autoplay is a gentle suggestion: you are not finished yet, there is always more, do not go back to your own life.

We call it doomscrolling, but the truth is more mundane. The feed is not a doom machine; it is a time machine. It shows us the future and the past in the same scroll, so we forget that we are sitting in a chair, in a room, in a body. The algorithm collapses time. It gives us the entire human conversation as an endless present, and in that endless present we are free from the ordinary pressure of duration. We do not have to wait. We do not have to be bored. We do not have to wonder what will happen next, because the next thing is already loading. And yet, somehow, the more we escape time, the less time we feel we have. There is a paradox: the infinite feed devours the moment we feed it.

Attention is a way of being in time. To attend to something is to give it your time. When we say “I don’t have time,” what we usually mean is “I will not give my attention to that.” Time is not money. Time is life. Attention is the currency we pay for being alive. You cannot buy back a single minute you spent not paying attention. The minutes are gone, and what remains of them is the residue of what you noticed. If you attended to nothing, the minutes leave no residue. They are simply erased. This is why a childhood of staring at screens can feel, years later, like a fog. It is why the memory of a long afternoon watching clouds is sharper than the memory of any show. The clouds did not try to be interesting. They were just there, and so were you.

Human beings are time-binding creatures. We are the only animals, as far as we know, that can think of ourselves in the past and the future. We live in stories. Our identities are narrative arcs: childhood, journey, loss, recovery. We arrange our memories into plots, with beginnings, middles, and ends. The brain is a storyteller, not a recorder. Every time we remember, we edit. We leave out what embarrassed us, we sharpen what flatters us, we smooth over the gaps. The past is a palimpsest, written and rewritten until it no longer matches the original. This is both liberation and sorrow. We cannot return to then; we can only tell stories about it. And the future is not a straight line. It is a branch, or a fan, or a sea. We cannot know it. We can only prepare, worry, dream, plan, and then be astonished by what actually arrives.

The present moment, the only point of power, is impossibly thin. It is like a razor edge between two infinities. We spend our lives walking that edge. Sometimes we fall into memory. Sometimes we fall into worry. The art of being alive is to stay on the edge without freezing, to feel the blade of now pressing against our feet and still take the next step. This is hard. It is especially hard in an age that gives us endless reasons to look away. But the present is all we have. The past is a ghost, the future is a guess. The only real thing is this, now, this sentence, this breath. And if you are truly here, in this moment, you may notice that it is enough. Not because it is exciting or comfortable, but because it is real. There is a strange peace in surrendering to the real.

I remember being a child, lying on my back in the grass, watching clouds. I had nothing to do. I was bored, in the way children were bored before the world learned to be afraid of boredom. But boredom is not emptiness. Boredom is the mind’s fallow field. It looks dead, but beneath the surface the roots are working. From boredom come daydreams, plans, jokes, poems. The child who is never bored loses something essential: the ability to be without a script. Modern culture treats boredom as an emergency. If we are bored for an instant, we reach for a screen. We have become afraid of the unscripted, the unpolished, the unfilled. We want our experience to be narrated from outside. But no one can narrate you. You are the narrator and you are also the character, and the author is asleep. What will you do with the silence? The question sounds like a threat, but it is really an invitation. In the silence, the self returns.

Language, too, is a silence we have filled with words. We are born into a current of language. It was there before we were, and it will be there after us. We learn the signs before we know the things. The world is given to us with names, and the names shape the world. This is a great gift and a great limitation. Consider the metaphor of time. In English, we speak of spending time, saving time, wasting time. Time becomes a commodity, a currency, a resource. This is useful in a world of schedules and salaries, but it changes how we feel. If time is money, then waiting is loss, rest is laziness, and boredom is bankruptcy. Yet in other languages, and in the language of poets, time is a sea, a garden, a wheel, a fire. The metaphor is not decoration. It is structural. We do not first see the world and then find words for it; we see through the words. To write freely is to try to see around the inherited words, to break the crust of cliché, to make the familiar strange again. This is why poetry matters. Poetry is language stretched beyond utility. A poem is a resistance to the commodification of speech.

There is a strange relationship between freedom and constraint. If you tell a writer to write anything, absolutely anything, the mind often goes blank. But if you say, write a sonnet in iambic pentameter, or write about this particular tree, or start with the line “The cold is a color,” then the hand moves. Form is not the enemy of freedom. Form is the container that gives freedom shape. The sonnet’s fourteen lines are not a prison; they are a dance floor. The constraint of rhyme gives you somewhere to go. The same is true in life, though we rarely see it. Absolute freedom is terrifying because it has no edges. It is like light in a room with no walls. We need boundaries to know where we begin and end. The body is a boundary. The earth is a boundary. The laws of physics are the original poems: strict, beautiful, impossible to break. Within their limits, everything moves.

I have been thinking about the body, and how much of our freedom is stolen when we pretend we are not animals. We live in controlled environments with controlled temperatures and controlled light. We have removed weather from our lives. We complain when it rains. We do not know the names of the trees outside our windows. The hands that type these words are animal hands. The breath behind the words is animal breath. The mind is an animal organ; thought is an animal activity. We are not disembodied minds floating through a digital cloud. We are mammals with the extraordinary gift of self-reflection, and the gift is not meant to separate us from nature. It is meant to be nature knowing itself. When we forget this, we become unwell. Anxiety, insomnia, depression, the strange rise of loneliness in an age of constant connection—these are symptoms of a species trying to live outside its own biology. We need the ground. We need the rain. We need to walk until we are tired and then sit under a tree and feel the wind on our skin. This is not escapism. This is return.

The natural world is full of attention. When you walk in a forest, you are being watched. The birds have noticed you. The squirrels have noticed you. The trees, in their slow way, have registered your passing. There is relief in being perceived as a moving animal, not as a profile. The forest does not know your name or your status. It knows only that you are alive and moving, and it responds accordingly. There is a quietness in that. The word “wild” comes from an Old English root meaning beyond human control. To be free is to be a little wild, to allow something in your life to remain unmanaged and unmanaged. We have taken the wildness out of our days and put it in our stories. But the wildness is still there, under our skin, waiting. It is not a dark primitive thing. It is a source of life. It is what makes you laugh without thinking, dance without reason, cry in the middle of a film because a character you do not know has lost something you never had. Wildness is unplanned meaning.

And meaning, if it exists, is made, not found. The philosophers say that the universe is indifferent, and they are right. But indifference is not the same as emptiness. The universe gives us raw material: light, time, flesh, weather. Meaning is what we make of it. We make meaning by attention. When you stop to look at the way the light falls on a glass of water, you are making meaning. When you remember a friend’s birthday, you are making meaning. When you say “I love you,” and mean it, you are making meaning. Love is the highest form of attention. To love someone is to attend to them, not to fix them or own them or save them, but to be present with them in their becoming. The opposite of love is not hatred. Hatred is a form of attention too, ferocious and consuming. The opposite of love is distraction. It is the glance away, the half-heard answer, the mind elsewhere. Love is hard because attention is hard. The world is always trying to buy our attention, but love insists on giving it away.

Death is the ultimate limit, and so it is also the ultimate source of freedom. Because we will die, our choices matter. Because we will die, the present moment has weight. A stone does not have a future that ends; it simply is. A squirrel, as far as we can tell, lives in an eternal present, aware of threat and food but not of the arc of a life. But we know the arc. We know that the story will end. This knowledge is both burden and gift. It is the burden that makes us anxious, and the gift that makes us alive. The Latin phrase memento mori—remember that you will die—was not meant to be grim. It was meant to be clarifying. It is a way of saying: do not wait. Do not save your tenderness for later. Do not put your beautiful work off until you are ready. You will never be ready. The only time to live is now. The only time to write is now. The only time to say what you mean is now, while the light is still changing and the tea is still warm.

Writing is a memento mori. It is also an answer. We write because we cannot keep anything, but we can shape something. A sentence is a small shape against death. It will not survive forever—no sentence survives forever, not even the ones carved in stone—but it can survive this moment. It can be a gift to a stranger, or to a future self who has forgotten who she was. The urge to create is the urge to say: I was here, and this is what I saw. It is also the urge to speak across the abyss to someone not yet born. Every act of writing is a letter to the future, and the future does not have to answer. The letter is enough.

There are two selves in every writer: the censor and the child. The censor is the voice that says “this is bad,” “who will care?,” “you missed your chance,” “that word is ugly.” The child is the voice that says “look at this,” “listen to that,” “why?,” “what if?” To write freely, you have to let the child play while the censor sleeps. Then you edit, and the censor wakes. The first draft is a way of seeing. The second draft is a way of caring. Many writers describe the first draft as downloading, and the second draft as sculpting. They are good metaphors. The blank page asks you to trust the child. The child does not know about grammar or market trends. The child knows the color of the light and the sad sound of a distant train. Good writing is the art of preserving childlike perception in adult grammar. It is never perfect. It is alive. A living sentence has a heartbeat. It is not a transparent window; it is a creature with skin and blood. When you read a good sentence, you know it in your body. It makes your chest tighten. It makes you laugh. It makes you look up from the page and see the room differently. The best sentences are not about words. They are about attention, and attention is a form of love.

So this essay has wandered. It has been about attention and time, language and limit, bodies and trees, love and death. But perhaps it is really about one thing: the strange, impossible, ordinary miracle of being here. To be here is to be a creature with a past and a future, standing on the razor edge of now. To be here is to be given a world that does not need you and yet is immeasurably enriched by your noticing. To be here is to have a voice, and a voice is the only instrument we have that can hold a moment still. We are all writing, all the time. We write our lives with the choices we make, the things we attend to, the words we say or swallow. The page is blank because we have not yet acted. Then we act. Then the page has a mark. Then the mark is our life.

I put my hands on the keyboard. The tea has grown cold. Outside, the light has changed again. It is deeper now, more gold than grey. The ordinary world is full of meaning if you attend to it. I have been writing freely, which means I have been writing with attention. That is the whole secret. Freedom is not doing everything. Freedom is choosing, attentively and lovingly, the constraints that make life possible. I choose this moment. I choose this sentence. I choose to be here, alive and aware, for as long as the now lasts. And if the now is thin, there is always another now after it. The pages turn. The tea cools. The light moves. The writing goes on. That is enough.

Title: "The View from Here"

It starts with the light. Late afternoon in November, ... The act of beginning any piece of writing is an act of faith: that something worth saying exists, that it can be found, and that the finding will not be forced. The blank page has a bad reputation. It is called daunting, intimidating. But blankness is also the purest form of possibility. A page with nothing on it can become anything: a love letter, a confession, a manifesto, a recipe, a lie. Then you type a word, and the possible becomes actual, and the actual is always smaller than the possible. This is the tragedy and comedy of making. To choose is to exclude. To write is to be forever haunted by the sentences not written. But the act—the humble, fingers-on-keyboard act—is the only way through. Freedom, perhaps, is not the absence of limitation. Then discuss attention economy. We carry rectangles of light that buzz and demand. Every app is a machine for harvesting attention, because attention is the substrate of desire. If you can control what someone notices, you can control what they feel, remember, believe, buy. We rage against "doomscrolling" but we are complicit: the pull is real. Perhaps we are not addicted to screens but to time collapse, the feeling that the future is happening now. The algorithm shows us the future and the past in same feed, so we forget that we are sitting in a chair, in a room, in a body. Attention is a way of being in time. To attend to something is to give it your time. When we say "I don't have time," what we mean is "I will not give my attention to that." Time is not money; time is life. Attention is the currency we pay for being alive.

Then memory and time. Human consciousness is a time machine. We are the only animal (as far as we know) that can think of itself in the past and future. We live in stories. Our identities are narrative arcs: childhood, conversion, journey. We arrange memory into plot. The brain is a storyteller, not a recorder. Every time we remember, we edit. The past is a palimpsest. This is both liberation and sorrow. We cannot return to then; we can only tell stories about it. What makes memory precious is its unreliability. We are not preserving the past, but composing it anew. And the future is not a straight line but a branch. The present moment—the only point of power—is impossibly thin, like a razor edge between two infinities. We spend our lives walking that edge. Sometimes we fall into memory, sometimes into worry. The art of being alive is to stay on the edge without freezing.

Boredom as capacity. Remember being a child, lying in grass, watching clouds, bored. Boredom is a state of suspended attention. It is the mind's fallow field. Modern culture treats boredom as an emergency. If we are bored for an instant, we reach for a screen. But boredom is not emptiness; it is a door. From boredom come daydreams, plans, jokes, poems. The child who is never bored loses something: the ability to be without a script. We have become afraid of the unscripted. We want our experience to be narrated from outside. But no one can narrate you. You are the narrator, and you are also the character, and the author is asleep. What will you do with the silence? In the silence, the self returns.

The world is given to us with names, and the names shape the world. This is a great gift and a great limitation. Consider the metaphor of time. In English, we speak of spending time, saving time, wasting time. Time becomes a commodity. This is useful in a world of schedules and salaries, but it changes how we feel. If time is money, then waiting is loss, rest is laziness. Yet in other languages and other poets, time is a sea, a garden, a wheel. The metaphor is not decorative; it is structural. We do not first see the world and then find words; we see through the words. To write freely is to try to see around the inherited words, to break the crust of cliché, to make the familiar strange. This is why poetry matters: it is language stretched beyond utility. A poem is a resistance to the commodification of speech.
